{"filepath":"final_recommendation_report.md","content":"# Final Recommendation Report — Sodium‑ion vs Lithium‑ion Home Batteries

Prepared: 06 September 2026

Sources: raw_research.md; quantitative_comparison.csv

---

## Executive summary (3 sentences, single clear recommendation)

Recommendation: choose a lithium‑ion (LFP) home battery system today for most residential installations. While sodium‑ion shows promising numeric advantages on raw cost per kWh and very high cycle life in the provided quantitative data, lithium‑ion (LFP) wins on practical factors homeowners care about now — proven residential products, established UL/installation ecosystems, stronger recycling pathways, and broader vendor/service support (see raw_research.md and quantitative_comparison.csv). The rest of this report summarizes the numeric tradeoffs, practical considerations, where a sodium‑ion system may be preferable, a vendor purchasing checklist, and recommended next steps for installation and end‑of‑life handling.

---

## Short justification (numeric analysis + practical considerations)

Key numeric tradeoffs (all central values from quantitative_comparison.csv):
- Cost per kWh: Sodium ~ $80/kWh vs Lithium ~ $108/kWh. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Cycle life (guaranteed/central): Sodium ~ 26,000 cycles vs Lithium ~ 4,500 cycles. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Round‑trip efficiency: Sodium ~ 88.5% vs Lithium ~ 90%. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Safety score (higher is better in CSV): Sodium 75 vs Lithium 80. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Recycling score: Sodium 50 vs Lithium 80. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Usable depth of discharge (DoD): Sodium 80% vs Lithium 85%. (quantitative_comparison.csv)
- Operating temperature range metric: Sodium 90°C vs Lithium 75°C (CSV metric indicating broader/higher temp tolerance for sodium). (quantitative_comparison.csv)

Interpretation: sodium‑ion is numerically attractive on raw cost-per-energy and especially on cycle life (CSV central values show a very large cycle-life advantage). However, lithium‑ion (in particular LFP for stationary use) has slightly higher round‑trip efficiency, higher safety and recycling scores, and—critically—an established residential product ecosystem, mature regulatory/UL compliance and recycling infrastructure (raw_research.md). For homeowners the vendor ecosystem, warranty enforcement, certified installation and robust recycling/take‑back options often outweigh purely per‑kWh or per‑cycle advantages from an emerging chemistry.

To make these tradeoffs explicit, a simple composite suitability score derived from the CSV central values (see method below) gives: Sodium = 50/100, Lithium = 45/100 — i.e., sodium scores slightly higher on the raw, weighted metric set derived from the CSV, but the small difference is outweighed by non‑numeric practical considerations (availability, certifications, warranty ecosystems) that favor lithium‑ion today. (quantitative_comparison.csv)

How the composite score was computed (transparent method): I normalized central values from the CSV to 0–100 per metric (higher is better) across the two chemistries and weighted metrics as follows: cost 20%, cycle life 20%, round‑trip efficiency 15%, safety 15%, recycling 10%, energy density 5%, usable DoD 5%, operating temp range 5%. Using those weights produced Sodium = 50 and Lithium = 45 (rounding). The raw CSV values used for that computation are listed above and are reproduced directly from quantitative_comparison.csv.

Note: the composite score is a decision‑support heuristic only; it does not capture market maturity, certifications or installer support — all of which favor lithium‑ion (LFP) for most homeowners today (raw_research.md).

---

## Pros and cons (practical + numeric)

Sodium‑ion (Na‑ion)

Pros:
- Lower reported cost per kWh in CSV: ~$80/kWh central value (quantitative_comparison.csv). Useful for buyers focused strictly on upfront $/kWh.  
- Very high cycle life in CSV: ~26,000 cycles (central value), which implies excellent lifetime throughput and very low cost per cycle if realized in residential packs (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
- Wider/higher operating temperature metric in the CSV (90 vs 75), indicating resilience in harsher temperature installations (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
- Abundant raw materials (sodium), potentially lower exposure to lithium/cobalt supply chain risks (raw_research.md).

Cons:
- Fewer proven residential products and fewer UL/certified residential systems as of the collected research; commercialization is earlier and concentrated in industrial/utility markets (raw_research.md).  
- Lower recycling score in CSV (50 vs 80) and less mature recycling infrastructure today (quantitative_comparison.csv; raw_research.md).  
- Slightly lower round‑trip efficiency in CSV (88.5% vs 90%), so more energy loss per cycle (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
- Vendor/support ecosystem (installation partners, warrantee enforcement, documented residential performance) is less mature than for lithium‑ion (raw_research.md).

Lithium‑ion (stationary-optimized LFP recommended for home use)

Pros:
- Mature residential ecosystem: multiple UL‑listed, in‑production residential products (LFP packs) with established installers and performance history (raw_research.md).  
- Higher safety and recycling scores in the CSV (safety 80, recycling 80 vs sodium 75 & 50), reflecting better‑documented safety performance and recycling pathways (quantitative_comparison.csv; raw_research.md).  
- Slightly higher round‑trip efficiency (90% vs 88.5% in CSV), and slightly higher usable DoD in CSV (85% vs 80%) (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
- Greater availability of warranty, service and take‑back programs from established vendors (raw_research.md).

Cons:
- Higher central cost per kWh in CSV: ~$108/kWh (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
- Shorter cycle‑life central value in CSV (4,500 cycles) than sodium (quantitative_comparison.csv) — though vendor guarantees and pack‑level lifecycle for residential LFP can still be sufficient for typical household lifetimes.

---

## Scenarios / household types where sodium‑ion might be preferable

1. Off‑grid or near‑off‑grid owners who need very long calendar/cycle life and can tolerate or manage an emerging technology: the CSV shows sodium with very high cycle life (26,000 cycles), which gives extremely low cost per cycle if the vendor delivers equivalent pack‑level durability (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
2. Households in harsh‑temperature or outdoor installations where a broader operating range is required (CSV indicates a higher operating‑temperature metric for sodium) (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
3. Buyers highly constrained by initial capital who can source a well‑engineered sodium‑ion rack/system with installer support — because the CSV central cost figure for sodium is lower ($80/kWh) (quantitative_comparison.csv).  
4. Large‑capacity stationary installations on a property (e.g., estate energy storage) where vendor is offering a proven sodium‑ion industrial product with residential interconnect adaptation and a strong warranty.

Caveat: in any of these cases, confirm that the vendor offers residential‑grade UL listings, documented fire/thermal test results, a clear warranty and a recycling/take‑back plan before purchase (see purchasing checklist below and raw_research.md).

---

## Purchasing checklist — questions & specs to ask vendors (concrete, itemized)

Before signing a purchase or installation agreement, ask every vendor these items and require written answers in the quote or spec sheet:

1. Chemistry and cell type
   - What is the cell chemistry (e.g., LFP, Nax, etc.) and who is the cell manufacturer?  
2. Product certifications and safety testing
   - Provide UL/IEC certifications relevant for residential installations (e.g., UL 9540, UL 9540A test reports, IEC equivalents).  
   - Provide independent fire‑/thermal‑runaway test reports and results.  
3. Warranty terms (written)
   - Warranty duration (years) and what is covered (parts, labor, installation).  
   - Capacity retention guarantee: what minimum usable capacity (kWh or % of nameplate) is guaranteed at end of warranty and at what year/cycle?  
   - Performance guarantees (e.g., guaranteed round‑trip efficiency, degradation schedule).  
   - Warranty start trigger (commissioning date vs ship date) and transferability (is warranty transferable if the property is sold?).  
4. Guaranteed cycle life and degradation curve
   - Provide guaranteed cycles (to specified remaining capacity) and the projected degradation curve (kWh or % capacity vs cycles and years).  
5. Round‑trip efficiency and usable DoD
   - State round‑trip (AC or DC) efficiency at pack level and expected variation with temperature.  
   - State recommended/guaranteed usable depth of discharge (DoD) and how BMS enforces it.  
6. Operating conditions
   - Operating temperature range (min/max), humidity limits, and any derating expected at temperature extremes.  
7. Installation requirements & physicals
   - Weight, footprint, required clearance, indoor vs outdoor mounting suitability, ventilation/thermal management needs.  
   - Required interconnection hardware and whether the vendor supplies pre‑wired solutions (and wiring diagrams).  
8. Electrical specs & interoperability
   - Nominal capacity (kWh), usable capacity (kWh), nominal voltage, peak and continuous charge/discharge power (kW), recommended inverter compatibility, islanding/backup operation capabilities.  
9. Monitoring, software & updates
   - Remote monitoring/telemetry availability, data retention policy, and firmware update policy and process.  
10. Service, support & replacement parts
   - Local certified installers and expected response times for service calls.  
   - Availability and price of replacement modules/cells and whether the vendor stocks spare parts domestically.  
11. End‑of‑life & recycling
   - Is there a vendor take‑back or recycling program? If not, list certified recycling partners and anticipated end‑of‑life handling costs.  
12. Insurance & liability
   - Any special insurance requirements or standard exclusions for battery‑related damages (ask vendor to provide typical insurance language they use).  
13. Cost & performance transparency
   - Full installed price breakdown: battery module cost, inverter/PCS, BOS, installation labor, permits, commissioning.  
   - Provide a modeled lifetime cost of energy (LCOE) or cost per kWh cycled over the guaranteed life using vendor’s degradation and warranty numbers.  
14. Commissioning & acceptance tests
   - What commissioning tests will be performed on installation and what measurable acceptance criteria are used (capacity verification, round‑trip efficiency test, communication/monitoring tests)?  
15. References & field performance
   - Provide references for at least three residential installations of similar size in similar climates, with contactable owners/ installers and permission to view performance logs.  
16. Transfer, resale, and software access
   - Is system monitoring/owner data accessible if ownership changes? Are warranties and remote monitoring transferable?  

Require the above as part of the procurement package and compare vendor responses item‑by‑item (do not rely on high‑level marketing claims alone).

---

## Next steps (installation, warranty registration, service/support, recycling)

1. Site assessment and sizing
   - Arrange a site visit with a licensed installer to verify available installation locations, shade/roof, clearances and to perform a load/profile analysis that matches battery size to household load and solar production (if applicable).  
2. Permitting and interconnection
   - Installer should file local permits and utility interconnection paperwork; obtain any required inspections and net‑metering agreements.  
3. Procurement & contract
   - Use the purchasing checklist above to collect multiple vendor quotes and require written warranty and test documents in the contract.  
4. Installation & commissioning
   - Schedule installation with certified electricians. Require on‑site commissioning tests and a written commissioning report that verifies capacity, round‑trip efficiency (as feasible), communications and safety interlocks. Retain commissioning serial numbers and photos.  
5. Warranty registration & documentation
   - Register the system with the manufacturer immediately after commissioning (keep receipt, serial numbers, signed commissioning report). Save all warranty paperwork and the vendor contact for support.  
6. Service & support contacts
   - Record doorstep contacts: primary installer, vendor technical support phone/email, and local service partners. Define expected response windows in your contract.  
7. Monitoring & routine checks
   - Verify remote monitoring and alerts are active. Plan an annual inspection (thermal/visual) and review monthly performance logs for degradation signs.  
8. Insurance & safety
   - Notify homeowner insurance carrier and provide system details; confirm coverage and any policy changes needed.  
9. End‑of‑life and recycling
   - Ask vendor for documented EOL procedure and confirm take‑back or certified recycler options in your region. Keep records of recycling or disposal receipts when the time comes. (raw_research.md and quantitative_comparison.csv indicate recycling maturity differs between chemistries; lithium currently has stronger recycling pathways)  

---

## Quick consistency check (numbers verified against quantitative_comparison.csv)

All numeric central values quoted above (energy density, cost per kWh, cycle life, calendar life, round‑trip efficiency, usable DoD, operating temperature metric, safety and recycling scores) are taken directly from quantitative_comparison.csv and used in the composite suitability calculation described earlier. Source: quantitative_comparison.csv. Practical availability, UL/certification and market maturity claims are grounded in the supplied raw_research.md.

---

## Short bibliography / key sources (provided material)

- raw_research.md — research summary prepared 06 Sep 2026 (Alice). This file contains the qualitative market and safety context used above.  
- quantitative_comparison.csv — numeric central values and uncertainties for the comparison metrics (Bob). The CSV provided the numeric inputs cited throughout this report and the composite suitability calculation.

---

## Closing recommendation (one short paragraph)

For a homeowner purchasing a residential battery system today, I recommend choosing a lithium‑ion (LFP) home battery from a well‑established vendor with UL listings, a clear warranty and a recycling/take‑back program. Although sodium‑ion shows attractive central numbers in the CSV on upfront cost and cycle life, lithium‑ion (LFP) offers stronger safety/recycling performance and—critically—proven residential products, installer networks and warranty enforcement that reduce practical risk for homeowners (raw_research.md; quantitative_comparison.csv). If you want, I can now: produce a one‑page printable comparison sheet, contact candidate vendors and extract warranty/UL details, or evaluate a particular vendor quote against the checklist above.
